x.ASV: Ho Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! add ye year to year; let the feasts come round:
x.Darby: Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city of David's encampment! Add ye year to year; let the feasts come round.
x.KJV: Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt! add ye year to year; let them kill sacrifices.
x.YLT: Woe to Ariel, Ariel, The city of the encampment of David! Add year to year, let festivals go round.

nt: ה֚וֹי אֲרִיאֵ֣ל אֲרִיאֵ֔ל קִרְיַ֖ת חָנָ֣ה דָוִ֑ד

Isaiah is speaking directly to the city of Jerusalem as if it could hear him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state whom he is speaking about. Alternate translation: [Woe is to Jerusalem, the city where David encamped]

Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express his distress about what will happen to the people of Jerusalem. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Disaster is coming] or [There is danger ahead for you]

Isaiah is using the phrase **Add year to year** as a common expression of the culture to mean “year after year.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Year after year] or [Every year]

Isaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not think that it will benefit you to add year to year, to let the festivals come around]

x.ASV: then will I distress Ariel, and there shall be mourning and lamentation; and she shall be unto me as Ariel.
x.Darby: But I will distress Ariel, and there shall be sorrow and sadness; and it shall be unto me as an Ariel.
x.KJV: Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be heaviness and sorrow: and it shall be unto me as Ariel.
x.YLT: And I have sent distress to Ariel, And it hath been lamentation and mourning, And it hath been to me as Ariel.

nt: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the celebration described in the previous verse and the distress that Yahweh will bring upon Jerusalem. Use a natural way in your language to indicate this contrast. Alternate translation: [Although the festivals come around, I will cause distress]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But I will greatly distress Ariel]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **mourning** and **lamentation**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will mourn and lament]

The terms **mourning** and **lamentation** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deep mourning]

The point of this comparison is that just as **an altar hearth** is a place where sacrifices are consumed by fire, so Jerusalem will be a place of bloodshed and destruction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [and it will be to me a place of bloodshed and destruction, like an altar hearth]

An **altar hearth** is a kind of raised platform where animals were burned as sacrifices to God. If your readers would not be familiar with what an altar hearth is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like the place where sacrifices are burned]
The word **Ariel** means **altar hearth.** If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote.

x.ASV: And I will encamp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with posted troops, and I will raise siege works against thee.
x.Darby: And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with watch-posts, and I will raise forts against thee.
x.KJV: And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.
x.YLT: And I encamped, O babbler, against thee, And I laid siege against thee--a camp. And I raised up against thee bulwarks.

nt: Here and throughout verses 3-5 of this chapter, the word **you** is feminine singular because it refers to Ariel, the city of Jerusalem, personified as a woman. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a circle** completely surrounds what is inside it, so Yahweh will completely surround Jerusalem with a besieging army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And I will encamp against you and surround you completely, as a circle surrounds what is inside it]

x.ASV: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust; and thy voice shall be as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.
x.Darby: And thou shalt be brought low, thou shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall come low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.
x.KJV: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.
x.YLT: And thou hast been low, From the earth thou speakest, And from the dust makest thy saying low, And thy voice hath been from the earth, As one having a familiar spirit, And from the dust thy saying whisperest,

nt: Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem’s humiliation were physically going down, as expressed by the phrase **become low**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you will be humiliated]

Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem’s humiliation were being brought down to **the dust**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your speech will be from a position of deep humiliation]

A **ritual pit** is a kind of hole in the ground that people used to try to summon the spirits of the dead. If your readers would not be familiar with what a ritual pit is, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a pit used to consult the spirits of the dead]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a ritual pit** produces a faint, eerie sound from underground, so Jerusalem’s voice will be weak and ghostly after its defeat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And your voice will sound as faint and eerie as a the sounds in a ritual pit from the earth]

Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem’s faint speech would **chirp** like a bird chirping from the dust. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your speech will be high-pitched but faint, from the dust]

x.ASV: But the multitude of thy foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones as chaff that passeth away: yea, it shall be in an instant suddenly.
x.Darby: And the multitude of thine enemies shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones as chaff that passeth away; and it shall be in an instant, suddenly.
x.KJV: Moreover the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones shall be as chaff that passeth away: yea, it shall be at an instant suddenly.
x.YLT: And as small dust hath been The multitude of those scattering thee, And as chaff passing on the multitude of the terrible, And it hath been at an instant--suddenly.

nt: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between Jerusalem’s humiliation in the previous verses and the sudden destruction of its enemies. Use a natural way in your language to indicate this contrast. Alternate translation: [However, the multitude of your strangers will be]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fine dust** is light and easily blown away, so Jerusalem’s enemies will be quickly and easily scattered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [But the multitude of your strangers will be easily blown away like fine dust]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context. Alternate translation: [and the multitude of the terrible will be like passing chaff]

Isaiah is using the adjective **terrible** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [terrible ones]

The point of this comparison is that just as **passing chaff** is blown away by the wind and disappears, so the enemies of Jerusalem will be quickly swept away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [and the multitude of the terrible will be swept away like chaff that the wind blows away]

x.ASV: She shall be visited of Jehovah of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire.
x.Darby: Thou shalt be visited by Jehovah of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.
x.KJV: Thou shalt be visited of the Lord of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.
x.YLT: By Jehovah of Hosts thou art inspected, With thunder, and with an earthquake, And great noise, hurricane, and whirlwind, And flame of devouring fire.

nt: The expression **it will be visited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [he will strike]

Isaiah is speaking of **the flame of a devouring fire** as if it were a living thing that could consume things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a fire that burns up everything in its path]

x.ASV: And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her stronghold, and that distress her, shall be as a dream, a vision of the night.
x.Darby: And the multitude of all the nations that war against Ariel, even all that war against her and her fortifications, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision.
x.KJV: And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision.
x.YLT: And as a dream, a vision of night, hath been The multitude of all the nations Who are warring against Ariel, And all its warriors, and its bulwark, Even of those distressing her.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **a dream** is not real and fades away when a person wakes up, so the attack of the nations against Jerusalem will vanish suddenly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And it will suddenly vanish, just as a dream fades away when a person wakes up in the night]

Isaiah is using **a vision of the night** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a dream.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a dream during the night]

Isaiah says **all of the nations** and **all of the ones warring against it** as extreme statements for emphasis. He does not mean that literally every nation will attack Jerusalem, but rather that many nations will do so. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form of exaggeration or express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [a vast number of nations warring against Ariel and a vast number of the one warring against it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the ones bringing harm]

x.ASV: And it shall be as when a hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or as when a thirsty man dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; but he awaketh, and, behold, he is faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion.
x.Darby: It shall even be as when the hungry dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; and he awaketh, and his soul is empty; or as when the thirsty dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; and he awaketh, and, behold, he is faint, and his soul craveth: so shall the multitude of all the nations be that war against mount Zion.
x.KJV: It shall even be as when an hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or as when a thirsty man dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; but he awaketh, and, behold, he is faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion.
x.YLT: And it hath been, as when the hungry dreameth, And lo, he is eating, And he hath waked, and empty is his soul, And as when the thirsty dreameth, And lo, he is drinking, and he hath waked, And lo, he is weary, and his soul is longing, So is the multitude of all the nations Who are warring against mount Zion.

nt: וְ⁠הָיָ֡ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ יַחֲלֹ֨ם הָ⁠רָעֵ֜ב וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה אוֹכֵ֗ל וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֮ וְ⁠רֵיקָ֣ה נַפְשׁ⁠וֹ֒ וְ⁠כַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַחֲלֹ֤ם הַ⁠צָּמֵא֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה שֹׁתֶ֔ה וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה עָיֵ֔ף וְ⁠נַפְשׁ֖⁠וֹ שׁוֹקֵקָ֑ה

These two sentences mean basically the same thing. The second clause strengthens the thought in the first clause by repeating the same idea with different words. Isaiah is emphasizing that the enemies’ hopes of conquering Jerusalem will be completely unfulfilled, just as a hungry or thirsty person’s dream of eating or drinking leaves them still unsatisfied. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could combine these clauses and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And it will be like when the hungry dreams of eating but awakens unsatisfied, or like when the thirsty dreams of drinking but awakens still faint and longing]
וְ⁠הָיָ֡ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ יַחֲלֹ֨ם הָ⁠רָעֵ֜ב וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה אוֹכֵ֗ל וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֮ וְ⁠רֵיקָ֣ה נַפְשׁ⁠וֹ֒

The point of this comparison is that just as **the hungry** person dreams of eating but wakes up still empty, so the nations attacking Jerusalem will find that their hopes of conquest are completely unfulfilled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And it will be as when a hungry person dreams of eating but awakens, and his soul is still empty]

Isaiah is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a person who is hungry]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look, he is eating]
Here, **his soul** represents “the person himself.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he himself is empty]
וְ⁠כַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַחֲלֹ֤ם הַ⁠צָּמֵא֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה שֹׁתֶ֔ה וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה עָיֵ֔ף וְ⁠נַפְשׁ֖⁠וֹ שׁוֹקֵקָ֑ה

The point of this comparison is that just as **the thirsty** person dreams of drinking but wakes up still longing for water, so the nations attacking Jerusalem will find their ambitions completely unfulfilled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [Or like a thirsty person who dreams of drinking but wakes up still faint, his longing unsatisfied]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context. Alternate translation: [Or it will be like when the thirsty person dreams]

Isaiah is using the adjective **thirsty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a thirsty person]

Here, **his soul** represents “the person himself.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he himself is longing]
הֲמוֹן֙ כָּל הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם הַ⁠צֹּבְאִ֖ים עַל הַ֥ר צִיּֽוֹן

Isaiah says **all of the nations** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He does not mean that literally every nation will war against Mount Zion, but rather that many nations will do so. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form of exaggeration or express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the vast multitude of nations warring against Mount Zion]

x.ASV: Tarry ye and wonder; take your pleasure and be blind: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.
x.Darby: Be astounded and astonished, blind yourselves and be blind! They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.
x.KJV: Stay yourselves, and wonder; cry ye out, and cry: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.
x.YLT: Tarry and wonder, look ye, yea, look, Be drunk, and not with wine, Stagger, and not with strong drink.

nt: Isaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of what he is saying. He is not truly commanding the people to blind themselves and be amazed. Rather, he is condemning them for their willful refusal to understand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You stubbornly refuse to understand, and you have blinded yourselves]

The word translated as **Make yourselves wait** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Scholars have proposed that the original form may have been a similar word that means “Be amazed.” That would seem to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Be amazed and have amazement]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **amazement**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and be amazed]
שָֽׁכְר֣וּ וְ⁠לֹא יַ֔יִן נָע֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א שֵׁכָֽר

Isaiah is speaking as if the people’s spiritual stupor were them being **drunk** on wine and staggering from beer. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are confused and disoriented, but not because of wine or beer]

The pronoun **They** refers to the same people whom Isaiah was addressing with the commands in the first part of the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people of Jerusalem are drunk]

x.ASV: For Jehovah hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes, the prophets; and your heads, the seers, hath he covered.
x.Darby: For Jehovah hath poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes; the prophets and your chiefs, the seers, hath he covered.
x.KJV: For the Lord hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes: the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.
x.YLT: For poured out on you hath Jehovah a spirit of deep sleep, And He closeth your eyes--the prophets, And your heads--the seers--He covered.

nt: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Isaiah is speaking as if spiritual blindness were **a spirit of deep sleep** that could be **poured out** like liquid. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has made you completely unable to understand]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **a spirit** that is characterized by **deep sleep**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a spirit that causes deep sleep]

Isaiah is speaking as if preventing understanding were Yahweh having **closed your eyes**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he closed the understanding of the prophets]

Isaiah is speaking as if the prophets were the **eyes** of the nation, since prophets enable the people to perceive spiritual truth just as eyes enable a person to see. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your eyes, the prophets, those who enable you to perceive spiritual truth]

Isaiah is speaking as if preventing the seers from receiving visions were having **covered your heads**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he has prevented the seers from seeing]

Isaiah is speaking as if the seers were the **heads** of the nation, since seers guide the people spiritually just as the head directs the body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your leaders, the seers]

x.ASV: And all vision is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee; and he saith, I cannot, for it is sealed:
x.Darby: And the whole vision is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which they give to one that can read, saying, Read this, I pray thee; and he saith, I cannot, for it is sealed.
x.KJV: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed:
x.YLT: And the vision of the whole is to you, As words of the sealed book, That they give unto one knowing books, Saying, `Read this, we pray thee,' And he hath said, `I am not able, for it is sealed;'

nt: The expression **a sealed scroll** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a scroll that a person sealed]

Isaiah is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone gives it to one knowing writing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vision**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all that the prophets have seen]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the words of a sealed scroll** cannot be read because the scroll is closed, so the prophetic vision cannot be understood because Yahweh has made the people unable to comprehend it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [like the words of a sealed scroll that no one can understand]

The expression **sealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a scroll someone sealed]

x.ASV: and the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee; and he saith, I am not learned.
x.Darby: And they give the book to him that cannot read, saying, Read this, I pray thee; and he saith, I cannot read.
x.KJV: And the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned.
x.YLT: And the book is given to him who hath not known books, Saying, `Read this, we pray thee,' And he hath said, `I have not known books.'

nt: The expression **the scroll is given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Or someone gives the scroll]

x.ASV: And the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw nigh unto me, and with their mouth and with their lips do honor me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which hath been taught them;
x.Darby: And the Lord saith, Forasmuch as this people draw near with their mouth, and honour me with their lips, but their heart is removed far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught of men;
x.KJV: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:
x.YLT: And the Lord saith: Because drawn near hath this people, with its mouth, And with its lips they have honoured Me, And its heart it hath put far off from Me, And their fear of Me is--A precept of men is taught!

nt: Here, **its mouth** represents “what they say.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [this people approaches with their words]
בְּ⁠פִ֤י⁠ו וּ⁠בִ⁠שְׂפָתָי⁠ו֙ כִּבְּד֔וּ⁠נִי וְ⁠לִבּ֖⁠וֹ רִחַ֣ק מִמֶּ֑⁠נִּי וַ⁠תְּהִ֤י יִרְאָתָ⁠ם֙

The pronouns **its** and **their** refer to the collective **people** mentioned earlier in the verse. Isaiah shifts between singular and plural forms because he is treating the people both as a single group and as individuals. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [with the people’s mouth and they honor me with the people’s lips, but the people’s heart is far from me and their fearing of]

Here, **its lips** represents “what they say.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they honor me with what they say]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s lack of true devotion were their **heart** being physically **far** from him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but inwardly they are not devoted to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fearing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way they fear me]

The expression **a taught commandment** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a commandment that men have taught them]

x.ASV: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid.
x.Darby: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do marvellously with this people, to do marvellously, even with wonder, and the wisdom of their wise [men] shall perish, and the understanding of their intelligent ones shall be hid.
x.KJV: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid.
x.YLT: Therefore, lo, I am adding to do wonderfully with this people, A wonder, and a marvel, And perished hath the wisdom of its wise ones, And the understanding of its intelligent ones hideth itself.'

nt: The word translated as **therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [for that reason]

Yahweh is using **behold me, one will add** as a common expression of this culture to mean “I am going to add.” Someone using this expression would more commonly say “Behold me, adding.” Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a solemn pronouncement.
